desc:
Ecom Swift LLC builds a Kotlin library or Android SDK that packages shared code for reuse. You get a small, documented, tested module that you add through Gradle and can host privately or publish yourself.

## What is a Kotlin library or Android SDK?

A library is a module of code with a defined public interface that other apps can import. An SDK is a library meant for outside developers, often with extra docs, a sample app and versioning. Both let you write a feature once and use it in many places.

Typical examples are a networking layer, a secure storage helper, a payment widget, a custom chart view or a client for your own web service.

## Why shared code becomes a library

When two or more apps copy the same code, every bug fix has to be repeated by hand, and the copies drift apart. One app gets the fix, another does not. New developers cannot tell which version is correct. Copy and paste feels fast until the third app arrives.

A proper library gives that code one home. A change is made once, tested once and released with a version number. Each app then chooses when to update.

## How a library affects cost and quality

A library saves time on every future project, because the hard part is already done and proven. Teams ship features sooner, and bugs shrink because the same tested code runs everywhere. If you sell the library to other developers, the quality of its docs and examples decides whether anyone adopts it.

A small public interface is the key. The less you expose, the less you must support and the freer you are to improve what is inside. We cannot promise how widely a library will be used, but we can make it easy to understand and safe to depend on.

## What a good Android library includes

- One clear purpose per module, so it does not turn into a dumping ground.
- A small public API with sensible names and safe defaults.
- Unit tests for the main functions and instrumented tests where Android classes are involved.
- KDoc comments on every public class and function.
- A README with install steps and short usage examples.
- Gradle files that other projects can import without extra setup.
- A sample app that shows each feature in use.
- Version tags and a changelog, so every release is traceable.
- Consumer ProGuard or R8 rules when the library needs them.
- Publishing set up for a private repository or Maven, in the larger package.

## How we work

First we agree on what the library does and who will use it. If it comes from an existing app, we read the current code, decide what belongs inside and plan how your app will call it afterward. Then we build the module, write the tests and documentation, and check it by importing it into a clean project.

The Basic package delivers one focused module with tests and a README. Standard handles several related modules with KDoc, a sample app, version tags and tests across Android versions. Premium delivers a full SDK with a networking and error layer, publishing setup, a pipeline that runs tests, and a migration guide with a walkthrough call.

## Library habits worth keeping

**Do:**
- Keep the public interface as small as you can.
- Write the README before you share the library with anyone.
- Use semantic version numbers and record every change.
- Test on more than one Android version.
- Decide early who owns the repository and the release process.

**Avoid:**
- Exposing internal classes just because it is easy.
- Mixing unrelated features in one module.
- Breaking the interface without a migration note.
- Adding heavy dependencies that every user must then accept.
- Publishing before another person has installed it from scratch.

## Who this is for

A company with several apps that all contain the same code. A developer who wants to turn a useful component into a product for other teams. A startup that offers a service and wants an Android SDK to help customers connect. A team that needs an internal library to speed up new projects.

## What we need from you

Tell us what the library should do, share the existing code if there is any, and describe who will use it. If it must support Java callers, say so at the start. We work in a repository you own and never ask for your passwords. Access is granted by adding us as a collaborator to that repository.
